title: Nicaea II names the honor-signs: kisses, embraces, lights, incense—honor passes to the prototype
source_text: XI. Quae vero sint ista honoris testimonia, Imaginibus Christi & sanctorum debita, Synodus explicat variis in locis. Nempe, juxta ipsam, talia sunt, oscula, amplexus, item luminarium & suffituum oblatio. Istud colligere est ex iis quae leguntur in Synodi definitione, quae habetur initio actionis septimae. Ubi docet Jesu Christi, Deiparae Virginis, & omnium Sanctorum imagines dedicandas & collocandas in templis, & aliis locis publicis & privatis, non solum ut per hanc imaginum pictarum inspectionem, omnes qui contemplantur, ad prototyporum memoriam, & recordationem, & desiderium veniant, sed etiam ut illis salutationem & honorariam adorationem exhibeant, non, inquit, secundum fidem nostram, veram latriam, quae solum divinae naturae competit: sed quemadmodum typo venerandae & vivificantis crucis, & sanctis Evangeliis, & reliquis sacris, oblationibus suffituum & luminarium reverenter accedimus, quemadmodum veteribus erat in consuetudine adductum est. Imaginis enim honor in prototypum resultat, & qui adorat imaginem in ea quoque adorat descriptum argumentum. Tomi jam citati pag. 386.
pass_a_gloss: But what those testimonies of honor owed to the Images of Christ and of the saints are, the Synod explains in various places. Namely, according to it, such are kisses, embraces, likewise the offering of lights and of incense. That is to be gathered from what is read in the Synod’s definition, which is had at the beginning of the seventh Action. Where it teaches that the images of Jesus Christ, of the Mother of God the Virgin, and of all the Saints are to be dedicated and placed in temples and in other public and private places, not only that through this inspection of painted images all who contemplate may come to the memory and recollection and desire of the prototypes, but also that they may exhibit to them salutation and honorary adoration—not, it says, according to our faith, true latria, which belongs only to the divine nature: but just as we reverently approach the type of the venerable and life-giving cross, and the holy Gospels, and the other sacred things, with offerings of incense and of lights, as was brought into custom among the ancients. For the honor of the image results upon the prototype, and he who adores the image in it also adores the depicted subject. Tom. already cited, p. 386.
pass_b_english: Nicaea II lists kisses, embraces, lights, and incense as the honor owed to images.
Images stand in churches not only to remind, but to receive honorary adoration (not latria).
Honor paid to the image ‘results’ upon the prototype.

choices.why: Council’s named rites short of latria.
